title: Whose wife? (Mark 12:18–27)
hookLine: a trick question about seven brothers; he is God not of the dead but of the living

cards: Seven brothers, one wife, and another trap. This time it's the Sadducees, and Mark tells us straight away what they believed: they say there is no resurrection. Their story is built to make the whole idea look ridiculous.

The Law of Moses said that if a man died without children, his brother should marry the widow, so the family line would go on. So, they say: there were seven brothers. The first marries and dies, no children.
The second marries her, and dies. The third. All seven.
Last of all, the woman dies too. The punchline, in the King James Bible: "In the resurrection therefore, when they shall rise, whose wife shall she be of them?" A story built to end in a shrug.

teach.b: Jesus doesn't laugh along. He says: "Do ye not therefore err, because ye know not the scriptures, neither the power of God?" Two mistakes.

First, you're imagining the life to come as this life stretched out, with the same arrangements. When the dead rise, he says, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven.
God's power isn't limited to making more of the same. And notice the woman: in their story she's only a puzzle, passed down a line of brothers. He refuses to play.
Second, the scriptures. Have you not read, he asks, in the book of Moses? At the burning bush, God tells Moses: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.
By then Abraham was long dead, and still God names himself as his God. "He is not the God of the dead, but the God of the living."
If God is still their God, they are still his. Jews in Jesus's day debated this.
The book of Acts says the Sadducees denied the resurrection and the Pharisees confessed it; on this question, Jesus's answer sides with the Pharisees.
Resurrection is anastasis in Greek: literally standing up again.

teach.h: HE IS NOT THE GOD OF THE DEAD, BUT THE GOD OF THE LIVING.
teach.b: The Apostles' Creed puts it plainly: the resurrection of the body. How it will be, the text doesn't say. That it will be, Jesus is sure.

how: Christians confess "the resurrection of the body" in the Apostles' Creed, and at Christian funerals this hope is often spoken over the grave; some churches remember the dead by name in prayer, especially on All Saints' and All Souls' Days.

o: the soul floating free of the body forever
the dead standing up again, raised by God
coming back to live this same life again

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: I am the God of Abraham

s: all Jews in Jesus's day rejected the resurrection
the Pharisees taught it; the Sadducees denied it.
Jesus answered from the books of Moses
the burning bush: I am the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
Jesus said marriages continue exactly as now
they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels.

games.q: you're asked a trick question meant to make the resurrection look silly: seven brothers, one wife. whose wife will she be? what do you say?
o: you don't know the scriptures or the power of God.
no one's, because there is no resurrection.
games.why: "Do ye not therefore err, because ye know not the scriptures, neither the power of God?" and then: God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.

practice: Let one person you've lost come to mind, a grandparent, a friend, a parent, even a pet if that's where your heart goes, and picture them at their best, without rushing past the ache if it's there.
If you believe, you can hold them before the God of the living and let hope sit next to the grief; if you're not sure what you believe, simply give thanks that they were, and still are, part of you.

wordCard.voice: Resurrection. In Greek, anastasis, standing up again. Jesus says God is the God of the living.

orig.note: Greek: resurrection, literally a standing up again. ana, up, and stasis, standing.

carryVoice: Your line: god of the living. Still their God, so still his. Day two hundred twelve, done.
